full_judgment:
4. The learned Additional Sessions Judge on consideration of the evidence on record convicted the appellant Tauhid Alam as aforesaid. Being aggrieved by the said judgment the appellant has preferred this appeal. 

 5. In this case prosecution has examined 7(seven) witnesses and defence has examined 2(two) witnesses. At the out-set it is to be stated that in this case there is no eye-witness of the actual occurrence. Presently, we will discuss the evidence on record to see how for the prosecution has been able to prove the case against the appellant beyond the shadow of reasonable doubt. 

 10. In this case there is no eye-witness of the occurrence. The prosecution has brought in the evidence of 7 (seven) prosecution witnesses to show the fact of bad relationship between the husband and wife due to demand of dowry by the appellant and other facts and circumstances to show that Rashida died in the dead of night inside the house of the appellant. Coupled with it the prosecution has also brought in the material evidence to show that the death of Rashida Begum was homicidal and not suicidal as suggested by the defence. 

 11. Mr Shariful Haque, the learned Advocate appearing for the appellant submits that in this case the information that was given by PW 5 Khalilur Rahman has been withheld by the prosecution and the FIR Exhibit I which was lodged by the 51 of Police PW 1 Abdul Latif suo motu is hit by section 162 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. We are to see which is really the First Information Report in this case as contemplated under section 154 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. In this case from the FIR Exhibit 1 we find that the police got information from P W. 5 Khalilur Rahman that Rashida Begum was married to appellant Tauhid Alam and they were not keeping good terms since their marriage and Rashida Begum was missing from the house of the appellant. Over the same incident the husband also started a GD entry stating that Rashida fled away with ornaments and thereafter a U/D case was started by the appellant. On the basis of the information that was provided by Khalilur Rahman relation of deceased Rashida Begum and the U/D case that was filed by the husband, the police went to the place of occurrence, recovered the dead body from the water and suspecting something wrong sent the dead body to the morgue and after getting the Postmortem Report started this case suo motu on the basis of the FIR Exhibit 1. Thus we are to see in the facts of the present case which information is essentially the FIR in this case. From the facts and circumstances of the present care we 3rd that Exhibit I is really the FIR in this case. Whether a particular information amounts to an FIR or not is essentially a question of fact which is dependent upon the facts and circumstances of a particular case. In this case there were two vague and indefinite information in the police station according to which police went to the place of occurrence and subsequently lodged the suo motu FIR. Information in a police station may come from one source and more than one such information may be recorded at about the same time and it cannot be said as a matter of rule that since one information is earlier in point of time the later report is no FIR and should be excluded as being hit by the section 162 of the CrPC. In the facts of the case the police after getting the postmortem report and in view of the vague and Indefinite information was fully justified in lodging this suo motu FIR. Thus in the facts of the present case the submission of the learned Advocate for the appellant that the FIR is hit by section 162 of the CrPC is wholly untenable. The 'learned Advocate has also made a grievance that Ayesha, a charge-sheeted witness has not also been examined for which an adverse inference should be drawn against the prosecution under section 114G of the Evidence Act. In this case, we have found earlier that there is no eye-witness of the occurrence. Further prosecution is not bound to examine all the witnesses in a case and the learned Advocate could not show how she is a material witness in the case. Hence non-examination is not at all material in the case. The learned Advocate has also made grievance that the statement of a co-accused under section 164 CrPC. Exhibit 3 has been relied upon in this case. We find from the evidence that the learned Additional Sessions Judge has considered the evidence on record and in doing so he has considered the statement Exhibit 3 of accused Maksuda as he found the evidence on record in conformity with Exhibit 3. It is true that on the basis of the statement of a co-accused under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the present appellant cannot be convicted. However, we are to see independent of Exhibit 3, whether the prosecution has been able to prove the case against the appellant beyond the shadow of reasonable doubt. 

 12. From the evidence of PWs 3 and 4 we find that in the night of occurrence there was a quarrel in the house of appellant Tauhid Alam. Both these witnesses testified that the appellant Tauhid Alam was asking the deceased as to why she failed to bring dowry money. Thus from the evidence of these two witnesses we find that in the night of occurrence there was a quarrel between deceased Rashida Begum and her husband, the appellant Tauhid Alam regarding the dowry. PW 2 Ahmed Ali, the father of deceased Rashida deposed that he gave on two occasions Tk. 2,000 to the appellant and he could not satisfy the farther demand of his son-in-law for which he used to ill-treat the deceased. PW 5 Khalilur Rahman also deposed that the relationship between the husband and her wife was also not cordial due to the failure of payment of the dowry and he spoke about the Salish regarding the dowry. Thus on a careful consideration of the evidence of these witnesses, we find that the appellant was not keeping good relationship with his wife and that he was pressing for dowry money from time to time. Thus we find that the prosecution has been able to show a definite motive for the murder of deceased Rashida Begum. Though motive is normally irrelevant in a criminal case, but the question of motive in this care which is based on circumstantial evidence is an important element to prove the guilt of the appellant. In the present case the evidence on record shows that the husband was demanding dowry from his father-in-law and due to non-fulfillment of the same tortured the wife and this fact goes a long way in this case which is wholly dependent on circumstantial evidence to show the motive for murdering the wife. Further from the evidence of PW 7 who held post-mortem examination of the dead body swelling injuries were found in the neck and on the chest of the deceased. PW 7 found ante-mortem congestion with extra-vassated blood in and around soft tissues by the side of the injuries on dissection. If injuries were not ante-mortem then definitely those could not be found. He also denied the suggestion that it was a care of drowning and he stated that the injuries were ante-mortem and homicidal in nature. The learned Advocate for the appellant was arguing that since forth was found coming out from the nose of the deceased it must be a case of drowning. From the medical evidence we find that the doctor has stated in his cross examination that death was ante-mortem. He has also stated that in case of drowning there cannot be any blood in frothing. But from the evidence of PW 5 Khalilur Rahman we found that blood was oozing out from the nose, of the deceased. This witness also stated that Rashida knew how to swim. PW 2 Ahmed Ali, the father of the deceased also stated that there was bleeding from her nose. PWs 1, 2, 3 and 5 found mark of injuries on the neck and chest of deceased Rashida Begum. In the case of drowning such injuries could not have been found. Thus we find that froth was oozing out along with blood from the nose of the deceased. From this it might be that deceased Rashida Begum was not completely dead when her body was thrown into the water believing her to be dead, So it may be that as there was some life in her froth might be found coming out from the nose. Thus considering the evidence on record along with the medical evidence on record, we find that the death of deceased Rashida Begum is homicidal in nature. 

 13. According to the prosecution the wife was killed by her husband in the dead of night in the house of the husband himself. As against this the defence case is that the wife might have committed suicide or that she gets injury while she tried to run away from the house and fell into the water. We find from the record that the husband lodged a GD entry that deceased Rashida Begum ran away from the house with valuable ornaments. Police on investigation found this to be false. Subsequently the husband also filed a UD case. Thus in the facts and circumstances of the case the conduct of the husband indicates that he was suppressing the truth and was taking contradictory defence in this case. From the evidence on record we find that the appellant (husband) failed to give any satisfactory explanation as to how his wife died on the night of occurrence in his own house. Further, the conduct of the husband is not the conduct of a normal husband whose wife died of suicide. Thus, on a careful consideration of the evidence and other facts and circumstances of the case, we find that the learned Additional Sessions Judge was perfectly justified in convicting the appellant under section 302 of the Penal Code.
